final_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: for rigid frameworks at infinite dilution, the entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's linear size (Vol**(1/3)) is large relative to the largest included free-path sphere (lsd_p), because tighter geometric confinement restricts guest translational (and, by coupling, rotational) mobility. Formally: holding lsd_p fixed, adsorbates with larger Vol lose more entropy on adsorption; holding Vol fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_p impose less confinement and smaller entropy loss.
final_candidate.rationale: E02 and E04 report that smaller-pore frameworks (FER vs FAU; MFI vs FAU) show larger rotational/total entropy losses, i.e., confinement extent tracks entropy loss. E03 states adsorption entropy loss has both translational and rotational contributions. The descriptor encodes confinement as a dimensionless size ratio rather than an absolute pore diameter, so molecule size and framework pore size enter symmetrically. Proxy limitations: lsd_p is Zeo++ Dif (largest included sphere ALONG the free-sphere path), which is neither the global cavity diameter Di cited in E02 nor the bottleneck Df; it is used here only as a monotone accessibility-scale proxy under explicit assumption. Vol**(1/3) is a whole-molecule vdW size scale, not the radius of gyration compared in E06. Vol and lsd_p have zero_n = 0 across the 2361 training rows, so the ratio is finite everywhere and no physical zero is imputed or destroyed. The q-normalizations are fixed positive references; the ratio is dimensionless and the log-free form avoids any implicit equality threshold at ratio = 1. AV (mass-specific fixed-probe accessibility) is deliberately not used, since AV = 0 does not imply zero molecular adsorption space and a literal AV/Vol free-volume claim is not justified.
final_candidate.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis fails if: (a) at fixed lsd_p, entropy loss does not increase with Vol over the training support (e.g., planar or elongated molecules behave oppositely to compact ones of equal vdW volume, indicating Vol**(1/3) is a poor linear-size proxy); (b) at fixed Vol, entropy loss increases rather than decreases with lsd_p, or is uncorrelated with lsd_p once density or ASA effects are held fixed; (c) the ratio adds no information beyond lsd_p alone, indicating molecule-size scaling is spurious. A competing explanation to exclude: apparent trends driven by framework chemistry (e.g., cation sites) rather than geometry; the source conditions C2/C4 do not resolve temperature, loading, or framework chemistry, so geometry-only causality is not established by the quotes.
final_candidate.proxy_assumptions: Assumptions, not established causality: (1) lsd_p (Dif) monotonically represents the confinement scale relevant to guest mobility, even though it is not the global cavity diameter Di of E02 and not the bottleneck Df; (2) Vol**(1/3) monotonically represents the molecule's effective linear extent for confinement, though E06 used radius of gyration, a different quantity; (3) the E02/E04 FER-FAU and MFI-FAU comparisons transfer to this benchmark's framework population at infinite dilution; (4) entropy loss depends on the geometric ratio rather than on absolute scales alone; (5) retained adsorbed-phase mobility matters (E05), so immobile-adsorbate treatments are not the target regime.
final_candidate.boundary_behavior: Finite training support: Vol in [20.424, 161.144] angstrom^3 and lsd_p in [3.3452, 15.5604] angstrom, both with zero_n = 0, so the descriptor is strictly positive and finite over the whole training domain and covers the full train quantile range [0.0, 1.0]. No legitimate physical zeros of other inputs (e.g., PBF, PMI, SPAN, GeDi, AV) are touched, since none are used; no median imputation is applied. The descriptor scales smoothly and monotonically in both inputs with no singularities inside the support.

To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via $$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$ $$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$ where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as $$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$ where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. However, performing experiments for many molecule-framework combinations is impractical. Computational experiments of adsorption therefore make for an attractive alternative. Nevertheless, there remain caveats. For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. Although these simulations are numerically cleaner compared to experiment because they involve analyzing efficiently a greater number of molecule–zeolite combinations, it remains overwhelming to apply them to the millions of hypothetical frameworks. draft.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: for rigid frameworks at infinite dilution, the entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's linear size (Vol**(1/3)) is large relative to the largest included free-path sphere (lsd_p), because tighter geometric confinement restricts guest translational (and, by coupling, rotational) mobility. draft.rationale: E02 and E04 report that smaller-pore frameworks (FER vs FAU; MFI vs FAU) show larger rotational/total entropy losses, i.e., confinement extent tracks entropy loss. E03 states adsorption entropy loss has both translational and rotational contributions. The descriptor encodes confinement as a dimensionless size ratio rather than an absolute pore diameter, so molecule size and framework pore size enter symmetrically. Proxy limitations: lsd_p is Zeo++ Dif (largest included sphere ALONG the free-sphere path), which is neither the global cavity diameter Di cited in E02 nor the bottleneck Df; it is used here only as a monotone accessibility-scale proxy under explicit assumption. Vol and lsd_p have zero_n = 0 across the 2361 training rows, so the ratio is finite everywhere and no physical zero is imputed or destroyed. The draft's mapping of E02's cavity-diameter mechanism onto lsd_p is a proxy assumption, not a verified identity; the hypothesis wording 'largest included free-path sphere' should not be read as the global cavity diameter Di.

Vol**(1/3) is a shape-dependent linear-size proxy: the cube root of vdW volume equals a characteristic molecular length only under self-similar shape assumptions. E06 compared radius of gyration to available cage space, which is a different quantity; the draft acknowledges this but the mapping from Vol**(1/3) to the confinement scale in the sources remains unverified. Planar vs compact molecules of equal volume could behave differently (the draft itself lists this in falsification criterion (a)).

The hypothesis asserts that tighter geometric confinement restricts translational and 'by coupling' rotational mobility. E03 reports both translational and rotational contributions to entropy loss, but the coupling between a geometric size ratio and the rotational component is not established by the provided sources; E05 additionally reports that immobile-adsorbate RRHO treatments overestimate entropy losses and that retained adsorbed-phase mobility must be accounted for, so the direction and magnitude of the coupling are unverified mechanisms.

E02 and E04 are specific framework-pair comparisons (FER vs FAU; MFI vs FAU for linear alkanes) with temperature, loading, and framework chemistry unresolved per source_conditions C2/C4. Extending these pairwise comparisons to a continuous monotone relation across the benchmark's framework population at infinite dilution is an extrapolation; the reported percentages (38%, 20%, 3-fold) must not become universal constants.

final_candidate.name: span_to_bottleneck_ratio
final_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, adsorption entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's enclosing radius about its center of mass (SPAN) is large relative to the largest free sphere that can pass through the framework (lsd_f), because a spatially extended molecule rotating inside a pore network whose bottleneck is narrow has fewer accessible rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger SPAN lose more entropy on adsorption; holding SPAN fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.
final_candidate.rationale: SPAN is a heavy-atom enclosing radius about the center of mass, a coarse proxy for the molecular radius of gyration that source E06 used to qualitatively rank rotational freedom inside cages by comparing molecular size to available space. lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest passing free sphere, i.e., a bottleneck proxy, not the global cavity diameter Di; using the bottleneck rather than an included-sphere diameter makes the ratio conservative: two frameworks can share a similar cavity size (lsd_p) yet differ in connectivity, and only the passing bottleneck distinguishes them. The ratio is dimensionless (angstrom/angstrom), so no dimensional inconsistency arises. Limitations: SPAN is computed in the implicit-H/heavy-atom representation with legitimate zeros (54 training rows, e.g., single-site species), so the descriptor is exactly 0 there rather than undefined; Df is a hard-sphere geometric bottleneck and does not measure framework chemistry, flexibility, or the actual accessible rotational phase space; the enclosing radius is not the radius of gyration. The mechanism is motivated by reported cavity-size-rotation entropy comparisons (E01, E02, E04, E06), but the mapping cavity diameter -> lsd_f and radius of gyration -> SPAN is a proxy assumption, not an established relation.
final_candidate.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis predicts that, holding lsd_f fixed at a given native value, entropy loss increases with SPAN; if, within a fixed-framework subset or within narrow lsd_f bins, entropy loss shows no systematic increase with SPAN (or decreases), the rotational-confinement reading is falsified. A competing explanation to test: SPAN correlates with molecular size and hence with the translational entropy loss already captured by volume-based descriptors; if the SPAN/lsd_f dependence reduces exactly to a Vol dependence, the rotational/shape mechanism adds no distinct information. Another competing explanation: the ratio only tracks a hard threshold for pore entry (molecules with SPAN >> lsd_f cannot diffuse at all and may occupy different sites), in which case the descriptor measures accessibility class rather than graded rotational confinement.

To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via $$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$ $$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$ where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows. However, performing experiments for many molecule-framework combinations is impractical. Computational experiments of adsorption therefore make for an attractive alternative. Nevertheless, there remain caveats. For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. Although these simulations are numerically cleaner compared to experiment because they involve analyzing efficiently a greater number of molecule–zeolite combinations, it remains overwhelming to apply them to the millions of hypothetical frameworks. draft.name: span_to_bottleneck_ratio
draft.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, adsorption entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's enclosing radius about its center of mass (SPAN) is large relative to the largest free sphere that can pass through the framework (lsd_f), because a spatially extended molecule rotating inside a pore network whose bottleneck is narrow has fewer accessible rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger SPAN lose more entropy on adsorption; holding SPAN fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.
draft.rationale: SPAN is a heavy-atom enclosing radius about the center of mass, a coarse proxy for the molecular radius of gyration that source E06 used to qualitatively rank rotational freedom inside cages by comparing molecular size to available space. lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest passing free sphere, i.e., a bottleneck proxy, not the global cavity diameter Di; using the bottleneck rather than an included-sphere diameter makes the ratio conservative: two frameworks can share a similar cavity size (lsd_p) yet differ in connectivity, and only the passing bottleneck distinguishes them. The ratio is dimensionless (angstrom/angstrom), so no dimensional inconsistency arises. Limitations: SPAN is computed in the implicit-H/heavy-atom representation with legitimate zeros (54 training rows, e.g., single-site species), so the descriptor is exactly 0 there rather than undefined; Df is a hard-sphere geometric bottleneck and does not measure framework chemistry, flexibility, or the actual accessible rotational phase space; the enclosing radius is not the radius of gyration. The mechanism is motivated by reported cavity-size-rotation entropy comparisons (E01, E02, E04, E06), but the mapping cavity diameter -> lsd_f and radius of gyration -> SPAN is a proxy assumption, not an established relation.
draft.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis predicts that, holding lsd_f fixed at a given native value, entropy loss increases with SPAN; if, within a fixed-framework subset or within narrow lsd_f bins, entropy loss shows no systematic increase with SPAN (or decreases), the rotational-confinement reading is falsified. A competing explanation to test: SPAN correlates with molecular size and hence with the translational entropy loss already captured by volume-based descriptors; if the SPAN/lsd_f dependence reduces exactly to a Vol dependence, the rotational/shape mechanism adds no distinct information. Another competing explanation: the ratio only tracks a hard threshold for pore entry (molecules with SPAN >> lsd_f cannot diffuse at all and may occupy different sites), in which case the descriptor measures accessibility class rather than graded rotational confinement.

draft.name: span_to_bottleneck_ratio
draft.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, adsorption entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's enclosing radius about its center of mass (SPAN) is large relative to the largest free sphere that can pass through the framework (lsd_f), because a spatially extended molecule rotating inside a pore network whose bottleneck is narrow has fewer accessible rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger SPAN lose more entropy on adsorption; holding SPAN fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.
draft.rationale: SPAN is a heavy-atom enclosing radius about the center of mass, a coarse proxy for the molecular radius of gyration that source E06 used to qualitatively rank rotational freedom inside cages by comparing molecular size to available space. lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) is the largest passing free sphere, i.e., a bottleneck proxy, not the global cavity diameter Di; using the bottleneck rather than an included-sphere diameter makes the ratio conservative: two frameworks can share a similar cavity size (lsd_p) yet differ in connectivity, and only the passing bottleneck distinguishes them. The ratio is dimensionless (angstrom/angstrom), so no dimensional inconsistency arises. Limitations: SPAN is computed in the implicit-H/heavy-atom representation with legitimate zeros (54 training rows, e.g., single-site species), so the descriptor is exactly 0 there rather than undefined; Df is a hard-sphere geometric bottleneck and does not measure framework chemistry, flexibility, or the actual accessible rotational phase space; the enclosing radius is not the radius of gyration. The mechanism is motivated by reported cavity-size-rotation entropy comparisons (E01, E02, E04, E06), but the mapping cavity diameter -> lsd_f and radius of gyration -> SPAN is a proxy assumption, not an established relation.
draft.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis predicts that, holding lsd_f fixed at a given native value, entropy loss increases with SPAN; if, within a fixed-framework subset or within narrow lsd_f bins, entropy loss shows no systematic increase with SPAN (or decreases), the rotational-confinement reading is falsified. A competing explanation to test: SPAN correlates with molecular size and hence with the translational entropy loss already captured by volume-based descriptors; if the SPAN/lsd_f dependence reduces exactly to a Vol dependence, the rotational/shape mechanism adds no distinct information. Another competing explanation: the ratio only tracks a hard threshold for pore entry (molecules with SPAN >> lsd_f cannot diffuse at all and may occupy different sites), in which case the descriptor measures accessibility class rather than graded rotational confinement.

descriptor_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, the entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the adsorbate's out-of-plane thickness proxy (PBF) is large relative to the bottleneck free sphere (lsd_f). A molecule thick relative to the pore-window bottleneck cannot freely reorient within the cage or re-align to migrate between cages, so its rotational (and coupled translational) freedom is more restricted; near-planar molecules (PBF near zero) can orient along the pore axis and retain rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger PBF lose more entropy on adsorption; holding PBF fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.
descriptor_candidate.rationale: PBF measures mean heavy-atom distance from the best-fit plane and is the only untouched shape input capturing out-of-plane bulk rather than overall length (SPAN, GeDi) or volume (Vol). Prior rounds probed linear size vs included sphere (Vol**(1/3)/lsd_p) and enclosing radius vs passing bottleneck (SPAN/lsd_f); this descriptor isolates the thickness dimension, which plausibly controls orientational freedom in window-dominated confinement (E01, E02 report larger rotational entropy loss in smaller-pore zeolites). descriptor_candidate.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis fails if, holding lsd_f fixed, entropy loss shows no monotone increase with PBF (e.g., flat and bulky molecules of equal volume lose equal entropy, suggesting translational configurational volume rather than orientational freedom dominates), or if frameworks with large lsd_f still show large losses for thick molecules (indicating cavity Di or framework connectivity, not the bottleneck, governs rotational confinement). prior_formulas.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: for rigid frameworks at infinite dilution, the entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's linear size (Vol**(1/3)) is large relative to the largest included free-path sphere (lsd_p), because tighter geometric confinement restricts guest translational (and, by coupling, rotational) mobility. Formally: holding lsd_p fixed, adsorbates with larger Vol lose more entropy on adsorption; holding Vol fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_p impose less confinement and smaller entropy loss.

Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, adsorption entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the molecule's enclosing radius about its center of mass (SPAN) is large relative to the largest free sphere that can pass through the framework (lsd_f), because a spatially extended molecule rotating inside a pore network whose bottleneck is narrow has fewer accessible rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger SPAN lose more entropy on adsorption; holding SPAN fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.

For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. review_issues.explanation: The cited rotational-confinement evidence (E02) is framed in terms of average cavity diameter ('FER ~4.3 Å vs FAU ~13 Å; the average cavity diameter is a descriptor ... indicates the extent of confinement'), not a passing-bottleneck free sphere. The draft substitutes lsd_f (Zeo++ Df) for the source's cavity diameter; this proxy mapping is declared as an assumption but is not supported by any quoted source. E06 likewise compares molecular radius of gyration to available space in MCM-22 supercages (cage-scale), not window bottlenecks.

No cited source connects out-of-plane molecular thickness or planarity (PBF) to adsorption entropy loss. E01–E04 discuss pore-size/cavity comparisons for alkanes; E03 states translational and rotational motions contribute to entropy loss generically. The thickness-specific mechanism ('thick molecules cannot freely reorient or re-align to migrate between cages') is a plausible construction, not a reported finding; the hypothesis is conditional and unverified in this benchmark.

PBF is computed in the original implicit-H/heavy-atom representation. Mean heavy-atom distance from the best-fit plane does not count hydrogen protrusions, so for H-rich adsorbates (e.g., the alkanes dominating the training distribution, MW up to ~184) the steric thickness that would actually restrict reorientation in a pore window is systematically underestimated. The draft acknowledges this but the descriptor is retained as the sole thickness proxy.

PBF has 587 exact zeros out of 2361 training cases (~25%), which are legitimate planar-molecule values, not missing data. The descriptor therefore collapses a quarter of the training domain to a single value (0), so any monotone-in-PBF mechanism is untestable within that subset by this descriptor alone; the derivative check (nonzero_fraction = 1.0, perturbation 0.00463 Å) samples only off-zero points and does not exercise the zero cluster.

The quantity_role pairing mixes distinct confinement scales: heavy_atom_planarity (adsorbate, implicit-H heavy-atom geometry) against bottleneck_free_sphere_Df (framework, fixed-probe Ze++ metric). Df is explicitly NOT the global cavity diameter Di used in the source comparison, and the normalized q-ratio equal to 1 carries no physical equality meaning; the descriptor's numeric scale is therefore an artifact of the training references (PBF_ref = 0.231 Å, lsd_f_ref = 5.163 Å), not a physically calibrated confinement ratio.

The claimed coupled rotational-plus-translational restriction ('cannot ... re-align to migrate between cages') conflates rotational confinement inside a cage with inter-cage migration through windows. Diffusion/migration barriers (E06 notes interstage diffusion may not occur even at 450–850 K) are distinct from the infinite-dilution adsorption entropy target (Sgas - Sads)/R; the hypothesis transfers a transport-like picture to an equilibrium entropy quantity without source support for that transfer.

The knowledge graph contains no edge from cavity_rotation (or any mechanism node) to PBF; only lsd_f/lsd_p/PMI/GeDi/AV/Vol proxy edges exist. Absent graph edges are unknown support, not disproof: the thickness mechanism may still hold, but its proxy link is currently unevidenced in the provided relations rather than refuted.

Evidence E05 reports that treating confined guests as immobile under the RRHO approximation overestimates entropy losses and that retained mobility must be modeled; this supports the general relevance of residual mobility but provides no formula, no coefficients, and no geometric threshold. Source-specific percentages (38%/20%, E04) must not be converted into constants or thresholds for the descriptor.

Algebraic dimension check passes (length/length dimensionless after normalization), and the limit lsd_f -> positive_infinity gives descriptor -> 0 as expected. However, unit consistency does not verify the mechanism: PBF (mean heavy-atom plane deviation) and Df (largest passing free sphere) measure different geometric objects, and equality of their units does not license interpreting their ratio as a physical confinement measure.

draft_candidate.name: thickness_bottleneck_ratio
draft_candidate.hypothesis: Conditional physical hypothesis: at infinite dilution in rigid frameworks, the entropy loss (Sgas - Sads)/R increases when the adsorbate's out-of-plane thickness proxy (PBF) is large relative to the bottleneck free sphere (lsd_f). A molecule thick relative to the pore-window bottleneck cannot freely reorient within the cage or re-align to migrate between cages, so its rotational (and coupled translational) freedom is more restricted; near-planar molecules (PBF near zero) can orient along the pore axis and retain rotational configurations. Formally: holding lsd_f fixed, adsorbates with larger PBF lose more entropy on adsorption; holding PBF fixed, frameworks with larger lsd_f impose weaker geometric constraint and smaller entropy loss.
draft_candidate.rationale: PBF measures mean heavy-atom distance from the best-fit plane and is the only untouched shape input capturing out-of-plane bulk rather than overall length (SPAN, GeDi) or volume (Vol). Prior rounds probed linear size vs included sphere (Vol**(1/3)/lsd_p) and enclosing radius vs passing bottleneck (SPAN/lsd_f); this descriptor isolates the thickness dimension, which plausibly controls orientational freedom in window-dominated confinement (E01, E02 report larger rotational entropy loss in smaller-pore zeolites). Limitations: lsd_f is the passing bottleneck Df, not the global cavity diameter Di used in the source comparison, so the proxy mapping from cavity diameter to Df is an assumption; PBF uses the implicit-H/heavy-atom representation, so hydrogen protrusions are not counted and the steric thickness of H-rich molecules may be underestimated; legitimate PBF zeros (planar molecules) are preserved and give a finite descriptor value of zero, expressing minimal thickness penalty rather than a degenerate case; q-ratio equal to 1 is not a physical equality threshold.
draft_candidate.falsification_criteria: The hypothesis fails if, holding lsd_f fixed, entropy loss shows no monotone increase with PBF (e.g., flat and bulky molecules of equal volume lose equal entropy, suggesting translational configurational volume rather than orientational freedom dominates), or if frameworks with large lsd_f still show large losses for thick molecules (indicating cavity Di or framework connectivity, not the bottleneck, governs rotational confinement). The proxy mapping also fails if the implicit-H PBF systematically misranks steric thickness for H-rich adsorbates.
draft_candidate.proxy_assumptions: Assumed, not established: (1) out-of-plane heavy-atom spread is a usable proxy for the steric thickness that restricts molecular reorientation; (2) the passing-bottleneck free sphere Df is a usable proxy for the confining window scale in the rotational-freedom mechanism reported for cavity-diameter comparisons (E02), even though Df is not the cavity diameter Di; (3) the reported MFI/FAU and FER/FAU rotational-entropy comparisons transfer conditionally to rigid pure-silica frameworks at infinite dilution; (4) no fitted coefficients from the sources are reused.
draft_candidate.boundary_behavior: Finite training support: PBF in [0, 0.656] angstrom with legitimate zeros for planar molecules (587 training cases) yielding descriptor value 0, not an error; lsd_f in [0.857, 7.687] angstrom is strictly positive in training, so the descriptor is finite and well-defined everywhere on the training domain; no division by zero and no median imputation of physical zeros.
